cells.tense: You're at the bench and the work is deepening under your hands, and you know it's deepening.
cells.ask: Give one round of practice to the work alone this week — no audience, no deadline, just you and the difference between what's close and what's not — and see what sharpens when nobody's watching.
cells.core:
You stay with a thing long enough for it to teach you, and that staying is paying off. Each pass you make is finer than the last, and you can feel the difference — not because anyone told you, but because your hands know more than they did. When you step back you can see the whole shape: what the work is, where it's going, what still needs doing. That wide view doesn't pull you out of the work. It's part of why the work keeps getting better.

What you're free to feed next is sharpness. Time with the thing by yourself isn't leaving anyone — it's what makes what you bring back worth bringing. Take one round of practice this week with no one around to see it, and notice what gets clearer in the quiet.
cells.sheetLine: You stay with the work until it deepens, and you can see the whole shape while your hands are still in it.

cells.tense: You're already living at a mastery that hasn't arrived yet, pushing the work toward a standard that's still ahead of you.
cells.ask: Put one finished piece in front of people who'll enjoy it with you — not to be judged, just to be shared — and let their pleasure count as part of what the work is for.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead is the version where the work is finally good enough, and you're building toward it at a pace the work can't hold. Every pass becomes a correction, every session a verdict on whether you're there yet — and the mastery you're reaching for keeps moving because you keep setting it further out. The work doesn't get to be finished. It only gets to be not-yet.

The turn is toward other people. Not feedback, not a critique — joy that's shared. Show one finished thing to people who'll take delight in it alongside you, and let their delight be part of why the work exists. You don't have to stop improving. Just let one piece land somewhere before the next one starts.

cells.tense: You set the work down at some point and you're still standing where you left it.
cells.ask: Say one plain thing about the pattern you can see, out loud, to one person — not the whole picture, just one true sentence — and let that be enough structure for today.
cells.core:
There's a thing you know how to stay with, and you're not staying with it. You can still see the whole shape of it from here — that part never left — but the part where your hands go back to the work, that part stopped, and you've been standing at the edge of it since. It's not that you lost the ability. It's that you stopped arriving.

What brings you back isn't forcing yourself to want it again. It's saying the thing you can see. One sentence out loud about the pattern, to one person, and that's the whole act — a small claim of structure in the world. Clear, reliable structure makes things make sense in your presence. Start with one sentence and let the rest follow from there.
cells.sheetLine: You can still see the whole pattern. You've just stopped doing anything with it.

cells.tense: You're already reading the whole pattern and talking about it like it's reading you.
cells.ask: Take one thing you've been describing as the situation and say it's your read — one sentence that starts with what you see, not what the thing is doing.
cells.core:
You're already doing the thing — standing back far enough to see how the pieces fit, and then acting on what you see. That's happening every day. But when you talk about it, it comes out as if the pattern were obvious to anyone, as if you were just reporting what's there. The reading is yours. Naming it as yours hasn't happened yet.

Smaller than a grand statement of ownership: just letting one thing you've noticed be something you noticed. Movement from feeling, direction from genuine engagement — say one sentence about what you see and own it as your seeing. That's the whole act. The pattern doesn't need you to be humble about it. It needs you to be the one who said it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already reading the pattern. You just haven't said the reading is yours.
